header: MANS-HIS-203 · Physiology — plasma protein fractions, viscosity and hypoproteinemia, authored from the His Continuous Berlin Book 2026's own 'Lecture 5: Plasma protein level, structure & classification' block (p.108-111, printed footer p.99-102), printed keys. Three questions reuse existing live Kasr/AU concepts (albumin/oncotic pressure, gamma-globulin defense function, liver synthesis of albumin/fibrinogen/prothrombin/half the globulins); three new mints (electrophoresis as the separation method, fibrinogen as the plasma-viscosity determinant distinct from albumin/RBC mass, oedema as hypoproteinemia's earliest sign). Raw block is Q158-198 (41 items); most are near-duplicate restatements of the same handful of facts (average concentration ~7g%, albumin dominance, osmotic-pressure phrasing repeated 6+ times) or duplicates of facts this lane already authored elsewhere (intrinsic factor, sickle cell, albumin synthesis site, transferrin/transcobalamin, alpha-1-antitrypsin/emphysema, acute-phase proteins) — held, not re-authored.

questions.title: The dominant plasma protein
questions.question: The plasma protein with the highest concentration and the lowest molecular weight is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibrinogen is present at a far lower plasma concentration than albumin, even though its contribution to plasma viscosity is disproportionate to that low concentration.
explanations.B: Correct. Albumin is both the most concentrated plasma protein and the one with the lowest molecular weight of the major fractions. Its high concentration is exactly why it is the main determinant of plasma colloid osmotic pressure, holding fluid inside the capillaries against the outward pull of hydrostatic pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gamma globulins are a minority fraction by concentration compared with albumin, and their molecules (immunoglobulins) are considerably larger than albumin, not smaller.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a minor plasma protein fraction; its clinical relevance (a deficiency causing emphysema) has nothing to do with plasma protein concentration or molecular weight ranking.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transferrin is present at a much lower concentration than albumin and is named for its iron-carrying role, not for being the dominant plasma protein by mass or the smallest by molecular weight.

questions.learning_objective: State that albumin is both the most concentrated and the lowest-molecular-weight plasma protein, and connect that concentration to its oncotic-pressure role.

questions.title: Where gamma globulins are synthesised
questions.question: Which plasma protein is the one major fraction that the liver does NOT synthesise?

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception this question is testing for. Albumin is synthesised in the liver, one of the fractions the liver does make.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Fibrinogen is a liver-synthesised clotting-factor protein, not the fraction that escapes hepatic synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Prothrombin is also synthesised in the liver, alongside albumin and fibrinogen.
explanations.D: Correct. Gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) are the one major plasma protein fraction the liver does not make. They are produced by plasma cells (differentiated B-lymphocytes) in lymphoid tissue, not by hepatocytes — unlike albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin and roughly half of the other globulins, which the liver does synthesise.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception. Alpha globulins are among the roughly half of the globulin fraction the liver does synthesise; only the gamma globulins fall outside hepatic production.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gamma globulins as the plasma protein fraction synthesised by plasma cells rather than the liver, unlike albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin and the other globulins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer beside option, p.108, Q165/Q167 combined ('gamma globulins synthesised in lymphoid tissue' + 'plasma protein formed outside the liver = gamma globulin')

questions.title: Gamma globulins' defensive function
questions.question: The plasma protein fraction responsible for defence against microorganisms and their toxins is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Albumin's role is oncotic pressure regulation and carrying small molecules, not antibody-mediated defence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrinogen's role is blood coagulation, not defence against microorganisms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alpha-1 globulin (e.g. alpha-1 antitrypsin) has an antiprotease role, not an antibody-mediated defensive one.
explanations.D: Correct. Gamma globulins are the immunoglobulins, and they mediate humoral defence against microorganisms and their toxins by acting as circulating antibodies. This antibody-mediated (humoral) defence is exactly what distinguishes the gamma globulin fraction functionally from albumin's osmotic role and fibrinogen's clotting role.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Beta globulins include carrier and complement proteins, but the antibody-mediated defensive function specifically belongs to the gamma globulin (immunoglobulin) fraction.

questions.learning_objective: State that gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) are the plasma protein fraction that mediates humoral defence against microorganisms and toxins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer beside option, p.110, Q184/Q185 combined

questions.author_notes: Combines Q184/Q185/Q168's three restatements of the same gamma-globulin-defence/immunoglobulin fact.

questions.title: Separating the plasma protein fractions
questions.question: The method used to separate plasma proteins into their named fractions (albumin, alpha, beta, gamma globulins) is:

explanations.A: Correct. Electrophoresis separates plasma proteins into their albumin and alpha-1, alpha-2, beta and gamma globulin fractions. The proteins migrate through a supporting medium under an electric field at rates set by their charge, size and shape, producing the characteristic banded pattern clinicians read for fraction-specific abnormalities such as a gamma-region spike or an albumin-globulin ratio shift.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Centrifugation separates blood into plasma and formed elements (or separates particles by density and mass), not plasma proteins into their individual named fractions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osmometry measures osmotic pressure or osmolality; it does not separate proteins into distinct fractions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chromatography can separate proteins in a research setting, but it is not the standard clinical method named for routine plasma protein fractionation; electrophoresis is.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spectrophotometry measures light absorbance, used for example to quantify total protein concentration, but it does not itself separate the proteins into fractions.

questions.learning_objective: State that electrophoresis is the method used to separate plasma proteins into their albumin/alpha/beta/gamma fractions.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer beside option, p.109, Q174

questions.title: The plasma protein that sets plasma viscosity
questions.question: The plasma protein mainly responsible for plasma's viscosity is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Albumin's high concentration makes it the main determinant of plasma's oncotic (osmotic) pressure, but plasma viscosity specifically is set by fibrinogen, not albumin, despite albumin's much greater concentration.
explanations.B: Correct. Fibrinogen is the plasma protein mainly responsible for plasma's own viscosity. Although present at a far lower concentration than albumin, its large, elongated, asymmetric molecule disproportionately raises resistance to flow, so a rise in fibrinogen (for example as an acute-phase reactant) raises plasma viscosity out of proportion to its concentration. This is distinct from whole-blood viscosity, whose major determinant is the red cell mass.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gamma globulins are the antibody-mediated defence fraction; they are not the fraction that principally sets plasma viscosity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transferrin's role is carrying iron in the plasma, not determining plasma viscosity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Alpha-1 antitrypsin's role is antiprotease activity; its deficiency causes emphysema, not a change in plasma viscosity.

questions.learning_objective: State that fibrinogen, not albumin, is the plasma protein mainly responsible for plasma's viscosity, distinct from the red cell mass's role in whole-blood viscosity.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer beside option, p.110, Q188/Q190 combined

questions.title: The earliest sign of hypoproteinemia
questions.question: The first and most important clinical sign of hypoproteinemia is:

options.B: Swelling of the face and oedema

explanations.A: Incorrect. Jaundice reflects raised bilirubin, not a fall in plasma protein.
explanations.B: Correct. When total plasma protein falls — chiefly albumin, the main determinant of plasma colloid osmotic pressure — the reduced oncotic pull can no longer hold fluid inside the capillaries against hydrostatic pressure, so fluid shifts into the interstitial space. Facial and dependent oedema is therefore the earliest and most clinically important sign of hypoproteinemia, seen for example in nephrotic syndrome, chronic liver disease and severe protein malnutrition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A bleeding tendency can follow from low levels of specific clotting-factor proteins (e.g. fibrinogen, prothrombin) in severe liver disease, but it is not the first or most characteristic sign of hypoproteinemia in general — oedema is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cyanosis reflects deoxygenated haemoglobin, unrelated to plasma protein level.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Muscle wasting can accompany severe, prolonged protein malnutrition, but it is a later, structural consequence, not the first clinical sign that follows directly from the drop in oncotic pressure.

questions.learning_objective: State that oedema, from the fall in plasma colloid osmotic pressure, is the earliest and most important clinical sign of hypoproteinemia.

questions.title: What plasma proteins buffer blood with
questions.question: Plasma proteins contribute about 15% of blood's buffering power through their dissociable acidic and basic groups. The single most important contributor to this buffering capacity is:

options.A: The imidazole group of histidine residues
options.B: The thiol group of cysteine residues
options.C: The epsilon-amino group of lysine residues
options.D: The carboxyl group of aspartate residues
options.E: The guanidino group of arginine residues

explanations.A: Correct. Histidine's imidazole group has a pKa close to physiological blood pH, which lets it accept and donate protons readily across the pH range blood actually operates in. This is what makes it the single largest contributor to plasma protein buffering, ahead of the other ionisable acidic and basic groups also present on the protein.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cysteine's thiol group is mainly involved in disulfide-bond formation for protein structure, not in blood buffering — its pKa is well above physiological pH, so it stays largely undissociated at blood pH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysine's epsilon-amino group is a basic group and does contribute some buffering capacity, but its pKa is well above physiological pH, so it is far less effective across the blood's actual pH range than histidine's imidazole group.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aspartate's carboxyl group is acidic with a pKa well below physiological pH, so like lysine's amino group it is largely dissociated (not buffering) at blood pH — histidine's imidazole group, with its pKa close to blood pH, is the dominant contributor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Arginine's guanidino group is strongly basic with a very high pKa, so it stays almost entirely protonated at blood pH and contributes little to buffering there — histidine's imidazole group is the dominant contributor.

questions.learning_objective: State that plasma proteins provide about 15% of blood's buffering power, and identify histidine's imidazole group as the residue mainly responsible.

questions.title: Haptoglobin's specific role in iron homeostasis
questions.question: Haptoglobin, transferrin and ferritin are all plasma proteins involved in iron homeostasis. Haptoglobin's own specific role is to:

options.A: Carry iron directly in the plasma
options.C: Bind free plasma haemoglobin released by haemolysis, conserving its iron for recycling
options.D: Transport vitamin B12 in the plasma

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carrying iron directly in the plasma is transferrin's role, not haptoglobin's — haptoglobin instead binds free haemoglobin, not free iron itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intracellular iron storage is ferritin's (and apoferritin's) role, not haptoglobin's.
explanations.C: Correct. Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin released into the plasma when red cells haemolyse, forming a haemoglobin-haptoglobin complex that the liver clears rather than the kidneys excreting it. This conserves the iron in that haemoglobin for recycling, and is also why a fall in plasma haptoglobin is used clinically as a marker of intravascular haemolysis — the complex is consumed faster than the liver can replace free haptoglobin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 transport in the plasma is transcobalamin's role, not haptoglobin's, and is unrelated to iron homeostasis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Intestinal iron absorption is regulated by mechanisms such as hepcidin, not by haptoglobin, which acts in the plasma after haemolysis rather than at the gut.

questions.learning_objective: State that haptoglobin binds free plasma haemoglobin from haemolysis to conserve its iron, distinct from transferrin's plasma iron-carrying role and ferritin's intracellular iron-storage role.
